title: Private Set Intersection Mule Graph for Credit Unions
one_liner: Let hundreds of small banks and credit unions ask 'has anyone flagged this payee account?' without revealing customers or lists, using cryptographic private set intersection.
customer: Credit unions and community banks, sold through CUSOs, leagues and core processors, plus fintech sponsor banks.
problem: One account takeover can send 50+ ACH transfers to accounts at multiple banks, and each bank sees only its slice. Large-institution consortia dominate, and smaller institutions avoid sharing because of privacy, liability and competitive-leakage worries, even though information-sharing rules (314(b)) allow it.
solution: A pre-payment check API and core-integration widget. A payee's hashed account and routing data is checked via private set intersection against the pool of accounts members have flagged, returning hit count, recency and fraud category without exposing either side's lists. It adds burst alerts that notify other members when a takeover is in progress and automates the compliance paperwork.
why_now: Open-source PSI libraries and confidential-compute services have matured. The FBI freeze data exposed the cross-bank blind spot, Socure's $5.2B valuation shows the market's value, and FedNow adoption is reaching smaller institutions.
revenue_model: $500-5K per month per institution by asset size, and per-check fees for fintechs.
non_obvious_insight: Banks decline to share data because of liability and competitive leakage, not indifference. Cryptography removes the objection without asking anyone to trust a vendor with their data, and the network effect is regional, so a single state league can seed it.
first_30_days: Talk to a state credit-union league and recruit 5 pilot credit unions. Seed with confirmed-fraud lists they already hold, build the API on open-source PSI, and sign letters of intent for paid rollout.

title: Court-Ready Deepfake Authenticity Reports for Lawyers
one_liner: $500-1,500, 48-hour forensic reports on disputed audio, video, screenshots and voicemails, written to survive an authenticity challenge.
customer: Solo and small family-law, employment and criminal-defence firms, insurer special-investigation units, and HR investigators.
problem: Cloned-voice voicemails and fabricated chats now appear in custody and harassment disputes. The proposed federal evidence rules on deepfakes (901(c)) and machine-generated evidence (707) have stalled, and in June 2026 the Standing Committee sent 707 back for further study, so judges decide case by case. Bespoke forensic experts cost $5-20k and take weeks.
solution: A productised workflow: intake with chain of custody, multiple detectors plus provenance checks (metadata, C2PA, compression history, device and source-app fingerprints), review and a signed declaration from a credentialed examiner, optional testimony, and template motions on authentication for lawyers.
why_now: Cheap voice cloning has moved from fraud into family and employment disputes. The federal rule process has stalled, leaving a gap that judges and lawyers must fill with experts, and lawyers face sanctions if they present unverified AI evidence.
revenue_model: $500-1,500 per report, $2-5k per day for testimony, and a $299 per month firm plan that includes three reports.
non_obvious_insight: Detection accuracy is weak everywhere. The scarce thing is a credentialed human willing to sign under oath with a documented method. Productise the signature and the paper trail, and treat detectors as inputs.
first_30_days: Recruit three forensic audio and video examiners. Sell through local family-law bar associations and CLE talks. Publish three anonymised case studies and a report template reviewed by trial attorneys.

title: Lender-Required Benefit Records for F&I Add-Ons
one_liner: A 20-second, VIN-aware 'did this product actually benefit this buyer' check and signed record that indirect lenders demand as a funding stip, because California's CARS Act (SB 766) bans add-ons that provide no benefit and lenders inherit the exposure.
customer: Primary payer: credit unions and banks that buy indirect auto paper in California (dealer-management and compliance teams). Secondary: California franchised and independent dealer groups, at about $149 per store per month, when a lender tells them to use it.
problem: SB 766 becomes operative Oct 1, 2026. It bars charging for an add-on the buyer would not benefit from, requires clear disclosure that add-ons are optional, and requires dealers to keep records for two years. Lenders that buy the contracts carry Holder Rule and Rees-Levering exposure for what happens in the F&I office. Nobody outside the dealership can see whether GAP was sold to a buyer with 35% down, a 7-year service contract to a buyer with 6 years of factory powertrain warranty left, or prepaid oil changes to an EV buyer. The FTC's federal CARS Rule was vacated in January 2025, so states and private plaintiffs are the enforcement, and the April 2026 $78.1M Lindsay Automotive settlement shows the size of the downside.
solution: A lightweight web form and API that the F&I manager fills in per product during the menu. It auto-decodes the VIN (EV or hybrid, remaining factory warranty, tire type, key type). It pulls loan-to-value from the deal numbers and runs benefit rules per product, such as GAP with LTV under about 90%, a service contract that overlaps the factory warranty, maintenance on an EV, and key replacement on a keyless-start car. It flags mismatches, captures a one-tap 'customer chose this anyway, here's why' rationale, and outputs a timestamped PDF and JSON record. Lenders add it to their funding-package checklist. The rule library is the product and is updated per state as CARS-style bills spread.
why_now: SB 766 takes effect in three days (Oct 1, 2026). Federal rule-making is dead, so the compliance burden has moved to states and to lenders' third-party-risk teams. More states are copying California's language. The Lindsay $78.1M settlement in April 2026 made every dealer compliance director and every credit union counsel pay attention.
revenue_model: Per-funded-contract fee of $2 to $4 paid by the lender or passed to the dealer, or a $149 per store per month dealer subscription. Later, sell state-by-state rule packs and an anonymized benefit-mismatch benchmark to lenders and dealer insurers.
non_obvious_insight: Most dealer violations are not lies. They are menu autopilot. The DMS menu shows the same five products on every deal and the pay plan rewards penetration, so a mismatch happens without anyone deciding to deceive. The buyer who will pay for compliance is not the dealer, whose incentive is to sell. It is the lender, who holds the paper, gets sued alongside the dealer, and has the leverage to make a data field mandatory at funding.
first_30_days: Read the SB 766 text and the FTC's vacated rule for the exact 'no benefit' examples, and turn them into 25 to 30 explicit rules. Build a plain web form with no DMS integration. Cold-pitch compliance officers at 15 California credit unions with big indirect books through the CUNA/California credit union compliance channels. Offer a free 60-day pilot in which they require it from their 3 to 5 highest-volume dealers. Pre-sell 10 dealers at $99 per month using the line 'your lender is going to ask for this.'

title: Made-in-USA Proof Files for Relabeling Brands
one_liner: Audit-ready substantiation files and monitoring for brands rushing to claim 'Made in USA' after tariffs.
customer: Consumer and industrial brands with $5M-$300M revenue and retailer private-label teams, buying through general counsel or the ecommerce head.
problem: Tariffs make US-made claims valuable, but an unqualified 'Made in USA' claim needs 'all or virtually all' US content and processing under FTC rules, with civil penalties per violation and state-law class actions on top. Brands switch suppliers on cost and forget the claim. Suppliers cannot document origin per component.
solution: Software plus service that maps each SKU's BOM to component and labor origin, gathers supplier attestations and mill certs, scores the claim, drafts compliant packaging and listing language ('Assembled in USA with global parts', or percent US), monitors marketplace listings and supplier changes, and builds a defense binder.
why_now: A reshoring marketing wave, supplier switching under tariffs, and active enforcement risk. The same BOM data that supports tariff compliance supports the claim.
revenue_model: $3-15k per product-line audit plus $500-2k a month for monitoring. Retailer programs that require proof.
non_obvious_insight: The first legal casualty of the reshoring wave is the label. Brands that reshore partially and market fully carry hidden liability, and a file built once serves both marketing and customs defense. The buyer is legal or marketing, not customs, so this avoids the crowded tariff-software budget.
first_30_days: Scan Amazon 'Made in USA' listings for weak claims using public data. Send a three-page claim risk scorecard to the brands. Sell the first 10 audits at $3k with a partner advertising lawyer signing off.

title: Ceremony-as-a-Service for Direct Cremation Providers
one_liner: White-label the memorial gathering that low-cost cremation providers can't deliver, so families buy a $1.5K box of ashes plus a $3.5K send-off.
customer: Direct-cremation companies (online and storefront), hospices and community organizations. Families pay for the events.
problem: NFDA projects cremation at 63.4% in 2025, rising to 82.3% by 2045. Direct-cremation providers win on price but hand families ashes with no ceremony. Consolidators' chapels and $8K packages don't fit that customer. NFDA reports 58.3% of consumers have attended services at unconventional venues, so demand exists but no one owns the coordination.
solution: A 'Celebration Desk' embedded in the provider's checkout as 'add a gathering'. A coordinator plus software books non-funeral venues (breweries, restaurants, parks, boats, halls), catering, a celebrant, a slideshow, live-stream and RSVPs. Packages are fixed-price at $1,500, $3,500 or $7,500. It also handles scattering permits and follow-up.
why_now: Direct cremation share keeps climbing. NFDA says 61.4% of consumers are interested in green options. Consolidators are structurally pinned to a 58% cremation mix and 3%+ annual price increases and cannot copy an unbundled model. Venues have empty weekday capacity and live-streaming is now trivial.
revenue_model: Fixed package fee at 35-45% gross margin, 10-15% rev share from venues and caterers, and a referral or white-label fee of $150-$300 per booked event to the cremation provider.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders see direct cremation as the industry's price-war threat. It is really an unbundling that turned the ceremony into a separate, high-margin purchase that nobody owns. The providers who created it have no event staff, and the consolidators' chapels are the wrong shape.
first_30_days: Pick one metro. Sign one direct-cremation provider and ten venues. Coordinate the first five events by hand at about $1,800 each, offered through the provider's post-arrangement email. Photograph and price each event to build the package catalog.

title: Settlement Claim Autopilot for Ticket Buyers
one_liner: A privacy-first app that reconstructs a fan's ticket purchase history and files claims in ticketing settlements and refund orders, paid per validated claim by administrators and plaintiff firms.
customer: Settlement administrators and plaintiff firms, who pay per validated claim because they are judged on claim rates. Consumers use it free or pay a success fee.
problem: The FTC alleges $3.7B in resale fees from 2019-2024. Live Nation was found liable on monopolization in April 2026. In June 2026 the UK CMA ordered StubHub to refund 50,000+ customers, and World Cup ticket failures triggered class actions in New York and British Columbia. Claim rates in consumer settlements are typically low because buyers cannot reconstruct old purchases.
solution: Fans forward receipt emails or upload data exports (avoiding restricted Gmail scopes at launch). Local parsing rebuilds each purchase (event, price, fee, date) and matches it to open claim windows and prefilled forms. Sell it to administrators as a claims-acquisition channel, and keep watching for new live-events settlements.
why_now: A wave of ticketing liabilities is landing at once, and cheap models can parse messy receipts. Individual recoveries of about $30 are uneconomical for lawyers but work in batch.
revenue_model: $3-15 per validated claim from administrators and law firms, optional 10-15% consumer success fee, and later expansion to other settlement categories.
non_obvious_insight: The real buyer is the administrator or counsel measured on claim rate, not the consumer. Email receipts are better proof than memory, and automation turns tiny per-person recoveries into a scalable business.
first_30_days: Launch a landing page around the CMA StubHub refund order. Pitch 5 administrators and pilot one active claim. Test the receipt-forward parser with 500 users and negotiate a per-claim bounty.

title: Medicare GLP-1 Bridge Eligibility and Prior-Auth Navigator
one_liner: A 2-minute eligibility check and clinician-ready prior-auth packet for the $50/month Medicare GLP-1 Bridge, sold to caregivers, independent pharmacies and primary-care offices before the window closes in December 2027.
customer: Two payers. (a) Gen X adult children (45-58, household income often above $100K) who manage a Medicare-age parent's medications and pay $29 per packet. (b) Independent pharmacies and small primary-care practices that pay $79/month to stop fielding the same eligibility and prior-auth questions by phone.
problem: Medicare started an 18-month GLP-1 Bridge on July 1, 2026. It costs $50/month for Wegovy, Zepbound or Foundayo, but eligibility is a maze. It needs a BMI of 35 or more, or BMI 30+ with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, uncontrolled hypertension or stage 3a+ kidney disease, or BMI 27+ with pre-diabetes, prior heart attack or stroke, or symptomatic peripheral artery disease. Type 2 diabetes, sleep apnea and MASH disqualify you. So does having filled any GLP-1 under Part D in 2026. Prior authorization is required. Roughly 3.8M Part D enrollees qualify and about 5.9M are locked out, so sicker patients are routed to Part D copays of $200-600+ a month. One 68-year-old retired professor with BMI 42, a quadruple bypass and sleep apnea told KFF Health News: 'I'm obese, morbidly obese, BMI 42... And yet I can't get it.'
solution: A plain-language quiz built from the published Bridge criteria. It flags the traps, such as a 2026 Part D GLP-1 fill or a sleep apnea diagnosis. It outputs one of three routes: Bridge, Part D with an expected copay, or a manufacturer cash price (TrumpRx lists $149-$299/month). It then generates a prior-authorization documentation checklist and cover letter for the prescriber (BMI evidence, comorbidity codes, exclusion attestation). Pharmacies and practices get a white-label link and a shared queue of who is waiting on what. It stays plan-neutral: no plan enrollment and no commissions from carriers, which keeps it outside Medicare marketing rules (confirm with counsel).
why_now: The Bridge began July 1, 2026 and ends December 2027, so the demand window is 15 months and open enrollment starts October 15, about 3 weeks from now. CMS is also ending the Part D Premium Stabilization Demonstration after 2026. That subsidy had cut average premiums by $26 in 2025 and $16 in 2026, and about 24.9M people are in stand-alone drug plans that may face bigger 2027 increases. Oral options (Wegovy pill approved December 2025, Foundayo approved April 2026) widen the eligible pool. Nobody has built a workflow product for a program this new and this temporary.
revenue_model: $29 one-time per beneficiary packet (caregiver-paid). $79/month per independent pharmacy or clinic for white-label link, queue and templates. Optional $15 per completed PA-submission assist. Sunset risk is real, so design the engine to carry over to whatever CMS replaces the Bridge with (KFF flags a coming BALANCE model).
non_obvious_insight: The eligibility rules create a paradox where the sicker you are, the more you pay. Sleep apnea or diabetes disqualifies patients from the $50 Bridge and pushes them into $200-600+ Part D copays, which can exceed manufacturer cash prices ($199 Wegovy pen, $299 Zepbound on TrumpRx). That gap creates demand for a neutral router rather than another telehealth prescriber. Evidence: KFF's Bridge criteria, cost and start/end dates https://www.kff.org/medicare/nearly-four-million-medicare-beneficiaries-met-the-eligibility-criteria-in-2023-for-the-medicare-glp-1-bridge/ ; the excluded-patient quote, 5.9M figure and Part D copay range https://kffhealthnews.org/aging/medicare-glp1-bridge-weight-loss-drugs-coverage-exceptions-cost-access/ ; premium-subsidy end and 24.9M stand-alone enrollees https://www.kff.org/quick-insights/cmss-decision-to-end-temporary-subsidies-to-medicares-stand-alone-drug-plans-could-mean-larger-premium-increases-for-some-beneficiaries-next-year/ ; cash prices https://trumprx.gov/ . To verify: whether Medicare beneficiaries can actually use cash-price channels, and how those purchases interact with Part D cap accounting. One fetched source (Wikipedia) implies TrumpRx has Medicare-specific pricing, which conflicts with the site's consumer prices.
first_30_days: Week 1: turn the KFF criteria into a quiz and publish 'Do I qualify for the $50 Medicare GLP-1 Bridge?' pages timed to the October 15 open-enrollment spike. Week 2: post in Medicare and caregiver communities and pitch 10 independent pharmacies (NCPA-style networks) on a free white-label link. Week 3: get one primary-care practice to review the PA cover-letter template for clinical accuracy. Week 4: charge $29 for the packet. Target 100 paid packets and 5 pharmacies on $79/month. Keep it free of plan recommendations until compliance is reviewed.

title: Resident Proof for Two-Tier Tourist Pricing
one_liner: A privacy-preserving QR proof of residence lets towns, museums and transit charge visitors more and locals less without building databases or discriminating by nationality.
customer: Municipalities and municipal attractions, ferries and parking in overrun towns of 5-100K people (Italy, Croatia, Spain, Japan), then private attractions and restaurants offering locals-first pricing.
problem: Insiders think dual pricing is a legal and PR minefield, useful only in niche places. It is spreading (reported moves include Rome's charge for non-resident visitors at the Trevi Fountain and resident-versus-visitor pricing at some Japanese castles). The real bottleneck is verification. Each site checks IDs by hand, builds a one-off app or discriminates crudely.
solution: Issue a wallet pass from the municipal residents' register, first over the town hall counter and later through national digital-ID wallets. It discloses only 'resident of X'. Gates and apps verify it offline, and the same pass unlocks locals-first booking windows and discounts. The town gets analytics on non-resident flows to tune fees.
why_now: Venice's flat fee reportedly did not reduce numbers, so cities are turning to differentiated pricing. EU member states must offer digital identity wallets by the end of 2026, which makes selective-disclosure credentials mainstream. Resident backlash is at its peak.
revenue_model: Municipal SaaS of EUR 10-30K per year, EUR 0.01-0.05 per verification, and an integration fee per attraction.
non_obvious_insight: Pricing policy is not the bottleneck; identity is. Whoever standardises the 'resident' claim owns the tollbooth for every future visitor-management rule, including resident-first windows, non-resident caps and local discounts.
first_30_days: Approach one town of 5-20K people that runs a municipal attraction, ferry or car park. Offer a free 90-day pilot where staff issue passes at the town hall and verify them with phone cameras. Use mayors' associations to find the pilot, and have a lawyer confirm the residency-based structure is proportionate.

title: Youth-Slang Drift API for Safety Teams
one_liner: A continuously updated, human-verified lexicon and drift detector for Gen Alpha and teen slang, coded risk terms and grooming language, sold as an API to moderation and school-safety teams.
customer: Trust-and-safety teams at game and social platforms, K-12 student-monitoring vendors, school-safety directors, and moderation stacks inside AI toys and companions.
problem: Youth language shifts every few months. Classifiers trained on last year's data misread banter and miss coded terms for sextortion, self-harm and grooming. School monitors bury counselors in false alerts. As bans push kids into private chats and games, moderation teams are older and further from the language.
solution: A lexicon with context tags (benign, hazard, coded-risk; severity; platform of origin; age range), plus alerts when a term's usage or meaning shifts, delivered via API and a weekly briefing. It is built with a paid panel of consented 16-19-year-old language scouts (parental consent where needed) and linguists.
why_now: Age-gated platform tiers, bans and duty-of-care laws raise the cost of missed threats. Moderation is now LLM-based and needs fresh context that models lack. Volume and speed of Gen Alpha slang keep growing.
revenue_model: $2-15k a month per platform or vendor for API and briefings, plus custom lexicon builds.
non_obvious_insight: LLMs know last year's slang, so freshness is a data-supply problem. The moat is the paid youth panel and labeling process, not the model.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 teens (with parental consent) and 3 linguists. Publish a free monthly 'Gen Alpha threat lexicon' for trust-and-safety newsletters. Land 2 design partners, one school-monitoring vendor and one kids' game, at $1k a month each.

title: Dog Walk Plus: Wellness Checks for Isolated Seniors
one_liner: Turn the daily dog walk at an older client's home into a consented, structured wellness check with escalation, sold to their adult children.
customer: Adult children of independent-living parents who own dogs and live alone (the payer). Later: geriatric care managers, home health agencies, senior housing operators, and long-term care insurers.
problem: A dog walker is the only outsider who enters an older person's home every day at a predictable hour. I have found clients on the floor, and noticed early cognitive decline: the dog fed twice or not at all, pills left out, mail piling up, new bruises. Adult children call and ask us informally, we have no protocol, no consent, and no escalation ladder. Seniors refuse pendants and sensors but accept a walker, because it is about the dog and their dignity stays intact. The dog is also why many seniors delay going to the ER.
solution: A 'Walk Plus' plan built on a written consent from the senior. Alongside the walk, the walker does a 60-second structured check (a 10-tap list covering mobility, orientation, medications visible, food in the fridge, home temperature, bruises, mood, dog condition). Family gets a weekly text summary with trend flags. There is a clear escalation ladder (no answer at the door, then family call, then agreed non-emergency welfare check), and a pet emergency plan with keys and authority on file so that if the owner is hospitalized the walker becomes the dog's custodian. That prevents surrenders and removes the reason to refuse the hospital.
why_now: A large cohort is turning 65 and aging in place, home-care aide capacity is tight, and adult children are stretched thin as remote caregivers. Structured notes are now easy to summarize into a plain-language weekly update. Health plans and senior-service providers are looking for cheap ways to catch problems early, and a daily reason to enter the home is exactly what monitoring products lack.
revenue_model: Walks at $25 to $45 per visit plus a $29 to $49 monthly check-in fee paid by the family. B2B later: license the protocol and reporting to home health agencies and senior housing operators, and sell trend data (with consent) to long-term care insurers or aging-in-place programs.
non_obvious_insight: The dog is the Trojan horse that makes monitoring acceptable. A pendant says 'you're frail'; a dog walker says 'I'm here for the dog.' Walkers already do this informally and unpaid, so the product is less a new service than a protocol, a consent form, and an escalation path around something that already happens every day.
first_30_days: Convert existing senior clients (most walkers have three to six) with a one-page consent form. Build the check-in with a form and Twilio text summaries, no app needed. Partner with two local geriatric care managers who charge by the hour for the same visibility, and post in senior center and church newsletters. Target 10 paying families and track escalations as your proof.

title: Pre-Surveyed Superload Corridors for Data Center Freight
one_liner: A subscription library of continuously re-verified main supply routes for 100-400 ton transformer and switchgear moves, so heavy-haul carriers stop paying for a bespoke route survey on the same corridors every time.
customer: Heavy-haul carriers and project-cargo forwarders moving transformers, switchgear and generators to data centers and substations. Secondary buyers are EPC contractors, equipment OEMs and state permit offices.
problem: Every superload needs a route survey covering bridge ratings, turn radii, overhead lines, signals, rail crossings and escort rules. It costs weeks and real money, and it is repeated from scratch for the same handful of corridors from ports and rail heads to the same data-center clusters. Transformer deliveries are project cargo booked years ahead, and the domestic flatbed leg is at its tightest in years. The delay that kills schedules is rarely the bridge. It is the utility that needs six weeks and a bucket-truck crew to lift a line.
solution: Treat major corridors like military main supply routes: classify them once, then re-verify on a cycle. A survey crew captures mobile LiDAR, 360 imagery and pole-height data on a fixed corridor, then builds a route package with go/no-go strip maps and choke-point drawings. Each choke point carries the owner and the lead time to clear it (which utility, how many weeks, what it costs, which county road closures and escort rules apply). Sell annual corridor subscriptions, with an engineer-stamped per-move certification as an add-on. Recruit surveyors from retired combat engineers and route-reconnaissance veterans.
why_now: Data-center buildout is turning transformers into the pacing item. Industry reporting expects annual U.S. transformer demand to rise from roughly 1,500 units today toward 9,000 by 2030, with about 12 GW of capacity announced across roughly 140 projects for 2026 but only about 5 GW under construction. Forwarders now lock in manufacturing slots, ports and heavy-haul routes years ahead, and the trucking leg has a second lead-time problem.
revenue_model: Corridor subscription of about $15-60k a year per carrier per corridor, per-move engineer-certified route stamp of $3-10k, and data licenses to OEMs, developers and forwarders who want pre-clearance before quoting a delivery date.
non_obvious_insight: Route knowledge decays, and reuse is high. A few dozen corridors carry most loads, so a maintained library beats one-off surveys the way a pre-classified main supply route beats a fresh reconnaissance. The value is freshness (last verified date) and the choke-point ownership map, not the imagery. Carriers will trade permission to reuse survey data for a discount on their own move, which funds the first corridors.
first_30_days: Choose one corridor with a live job, such as a Gulf Coast port to a Texas data-center cluster or a feeder route into a Northern Virginia campus. Offer a friendly heavy-haul carrier a discounted survey of its actual move in exchange for the right to reuse the data. Use a rented or $30-40k rig (GNSS, laser pole, 360 camera) and 2 veterans with route-reconnaissance or heavy-haul permit experience. Package the deliverable, then sell corridor #2 to that carrier's competitors and to a transformer OEM's logistics manager.

title: Licensed Principal-of-Record for Financial Agents
one_liner: Buy a retiring independent insurance agency, then rent its licenses, carrier appointments and supervision layer to AI-agent builders that need a legally accountable entity behind every quote and bind.
customer: Startups building consumer or SMB agents that quote, recommend or bind insurance (later, money-movement advice), plus independent agencies that want to deploy agents under compliance cover.
problem: An agent that solicits or binds coverage is doing a licensed activity, but software has no license. Fifty-state producer licensing and carrier appointments take years, so agent startups avoid the vertical, use lead-gen workarounds, or run unsupervised. Regulators are converging on the idea that a licensed entity must own what the AI says (the NAIC AI bulletin has been adopted by roughly two dozen states).
solution: Acquire one or two small independent agencies (about 1.5-2x revenue, seller-financed) and inherit their resident and non-resident licenses, appointments and renewal book. Onboard agent builders as sub-producers. Provide the supervision layer: conversation and decision logging, rule-based disclosure and suitability guardrails, escalation to a licensed human reviewer, E&O coverage and regulator-ready audit trails.
why_now: Independent agencies are shrinking (39k in 2024 to 37k in 2026), so owners are selling. About 95% of commercial insurance is still sold by humans. Q2 2026 insurtech funding hit $2.44B with 99.1% going to AI-centric firms (Outmarket raised $34.5M at a $335M valuation). ISO's generative-AI exclusion (CG 40 47) is pushing buyers to look for affirmative cover.
revenue_model: A 20-40% override on commissions from agent-originated policies, a monthly supervision and platform fee per agent-builder ($2-10k), and the acquired book's renewal commissions as base cash flow.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input is not the model but a clean license history plus carrier appointments, which a retiring agency owner will sell cheaply and whose renewal stream funds the company. Whoever becomes the accountable principal for autonomous sellers collects a toll on all of them, a US analog to the UK Appointed Representative regime.
first_30_days: Shortlist 5 agencies (owners 60+, $500k-$2M revenue, licensed in 10+ states) through perpetuation brokers and sign an LOI with seller financing on one. Sign 3 design partners (AI quoting or benefits-navigator startups) for shadow-mode onboarding. Get a written opinion from insurance-regulatory counsel on how AI-conducted solicitations are treated for sub-producers in the first 3 states.

title: Auracast Hearing Access for Churches and Senior Centers
one_liner: Turnkey Bluetooth Auracast broadcast installs that let people with hearing loss hear services, meetings and group activities directly in their own hearing aids and earbuds.
customer: Houses of worship, senior centers, libraries, community halls and municipal meeting rooms, paying $1.5-6k for install plus $50-150 a month managed service.
problem: Hearing loss is a leading modifiable dementia risk and a quiet driver of withdrawal: people stop going to services, dinners and meetings because they cannot follow. Fewer than one in three adults who could benefit use hearing aids. Legacy hearing loops are costly and often fail unnoticed, and FM systems require borrowing clunky receivers. Venues with amplified sound face ADA assistive-listening obligations that many ignore.
solution: Pre-configured Auracast transmitters (line-in or audio-over-IP) installed in a day, with QR signage ('join the broadcast'), usher training, room-level coverage checks and a remote-monitoring dashboard so it keeps working. Multi-channel support allows a second-language stream (English and Spanish) from the same room.
why_now: Auracast (LE Audio broadcast) is shipping in current hearing aids, phones and earbuds. OTC hearing aids (2022) and AirPods Pro hearing-aid features (Sep-Oct 2024) expanded the user base. Loneliness is now a WHO-measured metric, and venues want visible ways to include older attendees.
revenue_model: Install fee plus recurring managed-service subscription. Referral fees from audiologists and hearing-aid manufacturers seeking demand generation.
non_obvious_insight: The hidden loneliness intervention is upstream of any program: tens of millions of people with hearing loss quietly stop attending. Fixing the room is cheaper than fixing the person, and Auracast collapses the cost of doing it.
first_30_days: Buy three transmitters (about $300-600 each). Install free in three churches or senior centers in one metro with an audiologist partner, capture attendance and testimonials, then sell ten installs at about $2.5k through denominational newsletters and audiologist referrals.

title: Founder File for Under-18 Hustlers
one_liner: A verified business transcript, tax pack and Roth IRA earned-income record for the parents of teens who legally can't hold the seller accounts their income runs through.
customer: Parents of 14 to 17-year-old sellers (eBay, StockX, GOAT, Whatnot, TikTok Shop, Depop, Shopify), high-school entrepreneurship programs (DECA, FBLA, Junior Achievement, NFTE), and college counselors. $12 to $15 per month or $149 per year, or $5 per student through programs.
problem: Most major marketplaces require sellers to be 18, so teens run their business under a parent's ID and account. The income, cost basis and reputation all legally belong to the parent. The parent gets a 1099-K on gross sales with no cost basis, which looks like profit. The kid can't prove any of it on a college application, and nobody is documenting the earned income that would let the family fund a custodial Roth IRA (contribution capped at the lower of earned income or the annual limit, roughly $7,000 to $7,500 per year).
solution: Founder File connects read-only to platform exports, PayPal and Gmail receipts, matches purchases to sales for cost basis, and produces: (1) a signed Business Transcript PDF for Common App activity entries and scholarship applications, (2) a Schedule C-ready summary and quarterly estimates for the parent, reviewed by a partner CPA, (3) an earned-income letter and referral to Fidelity or Schwab custodial Roth accounts, and (4) an '18th birthday migration' kit to move history to the kid's own accounts.
why_now: The 2025 tax law rolled the 1099-K reporting threshold back toward $20,000 and 200 transactions, so many teen sellers land in a confusing gray zone about reporting. College admissions increasingly reward proof of real work as test-optional policies spread and AI-polished essays get discounted. Teen commerce through TikTok Shop, Whatnot and reselling is at its peak, and Gen Alpha hustle culture is pulling younger kids in.
revenue_model: Parent subscription, per-student pricing through school programs, and referral fees from custodial brokerage accounts. Possible upsell: CPA-reviewed tax filing.
non_obvious_insight: Teen resellers are among the most under-documented earned-income earners in the country. Documenting what they already do unlocks tax-free compounding worth thousands per kid and turns a bedroom hobby into an admissions asset. The buyer is the parent, who pays for college advantage without hesitation, while everyone else sells to the kid.
first_30_days: Recruit 30 teen resellers from the Discord servers I am in. Give them free transcripts in return for parent-approved testimonials. Have a CPA friend sign off on a template. Sell a $49 'Transcript plus Roth IRA setup' bundle to their parents, and offer the transcript to 5 college-counseling and 'teen entrepreneur' TikTok creators for an affiliate cut.

title: Farmer-Photo Crop Insurance Verification
one_liner: Replace satellite guesswork with dense, fraud-checked farmer photos, read by locally trained crop models, to trigger insurance payouts.
customer: Agricultural insurers and reinsurers, agri-input companies and cooperatives in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania.
problem: Western models fail spectacularly on African crops, index insurance has high basis risk, and manual claim verification costs more than a smallholder premium.
solution: A local crop-damage model trained on image datasets (one project has 5M+ crop images) that takes geo-tagged WhatsApp photos, cross-checks neighbouring farms and weather, and triggers mobile-money payouts. The wedge is one maize or coffee cooperative with one insurer.
why_now: Local crop datasets and small on-device models exist now, and FarmerChat has answered 8M+ farmer questions, so farmers already talk to AI on their phones.
revenue_model: $0.50-2 per policy per season for verification, or a share of premium.
non_obvious_insight: Basis risk is solved by dense ground truth from the insured themselves, not by better satellites.
first_30_days: Partner with a cooperative of about 2,000 farmers and run photo verification in parallel with existing claims for one season.

title: Independent Inspections for AI-Built Software
one_liner: A third-party inspection-and-certificate service, staffed by displaced senior engineers, that tells buyers, lenders and insurers what is really inside AI-generated apps before money changes hands.
customer: Buyers of micro-SaaS and small apps on acquisition marketplaces (deals $20k-$2M), SMBs whose apps were built by vibe-coding freelancers, seed investors doing diligence and lenders financing software purchases.
problem: Insiders say AI made software cheap, but the cost moved to trust. Marketplaces are filling with prompt-built products of unknown security, licensing and maintainability, and misconfigured database rules in AI-generated apps have been reported. Traditional code audits cost $10-50k and take weeks. Meanwhile senior devs sit unemployed for many months.
solution: A fixed-price 48-hour 'app inspection': automated scans (secrets, dependency licences, database access rules, auth and PII flows) plus a 2-4 hour senior human review. The output is a standardised graded report like a home-inspection report, with repair-cost estimates and a maintainability score. Inspectors are paid $500-900 each, and an optional badge can be accepted by escrow agents.
why_now: The vibe-coding boom in 2025-26 flooded acquisition marketplaces with AI-built listings, agentic scanners make the first pass nearly free, and unemployed senior engineers are abundant.
revenue_model: $1.5-4k per inspection at 40-50% gross margin, recurring contracts with portfolio buyers, and referral fees from repair shops.
non_obvious_insight: When production cost collapses, value shifts to attestation. Every asset that became cheap to produce (1970s housing, used cars, diamonds) spawned an independent inspector class. Nobody has yet set the trusted standard for AI-built software, and the inspectors' seniority is the moat, the same people the market calls redundant.
first_30_days: Offer discounted $500 inspections in acquisition-marketplace buyer forums and Indie Hackers. Recruit 6 laid-off senior engineers and run 10 inspections on live listings. Publish anonymised findings ('7 of 10 exposed user data') and sign one escrow or broker referral partner.

title: Battery Passport Onboarding for E-Bike and Storage Makers
one_liner: Done-for-you EU battery passport, QR labelling and supplier data collection for makers of e-bikes, scooters and industrial or stationary batteries facing the 18 Feb 2027 date.
customer: Mid-size e-bike, e-scooter and light-EV brands, industrial battery pack assemblers and BESS integrators selling in the EU (20-500 staff), plus importers who count as the manufacturer.
problem: The EU Battery Regulation requires from 18 Feb 2027 a QR code and electronic battery passport for EV, light-transport and industrial batteries above 2 kWh (background knowledge; verify current status and any slippage). The data spans composition, cell supplier, recycled content, carbon footprint and state of health, and it must be extracted from cell makers who resist sharing. Larger passport vendors serve automakers and big OEMs, so small assemblers fall through.
solution: A supplier data-collection portal with templates for cell makers, a passport record generator with public and restricted access tiers, QR label files, state-of-health data hooks, a compliance checklist and change updates, plus a service layer that chases suppliers until they answer.
why_now: About 20 weeks remain, delegated acts and standards are still in flux, and small makers cannot wait for perfect specs. Even if parts slip, buyers still need the underlying data.
revenue_model: EUR 8-30k onboarding plus EUR 3-10k/year platform per battery family, with supplier-chasing billed hourly.
non_obvious_insight: The passport is a supplier-data-chasing problem, not a blockchain problem. Small buyers can pool leverage as a buying club so a cell maker answers one questionnaire instead of fifty.
first_30_days: Compile 200 EU e-bike and light-EV brands via a trade body and email a 'passport readiness scorecard'. Sign five design partners at EUR 5k and negotiate a template data sheet with two cell makers.

title: CJIS 6.0 Identity Kit for Small Agencies
one_liner: A managed multifactor and identity-verification stack that works in patrol cars, radio dead zones and shared workstations, ready for the Oct 1, 2027 CJIS deadline.
customer: Sheriff's offices and police departments with 10-150 sworn officers and no dedicated IT security staff, plus the managed service providers that serve them.
problem: CJIS 6.0 requires MFA and identity verification by Oct 1, 2027. Generic MFA breaks on shared terminals, offline vehicles and old mobile data computers. Small agencies buy compliance piecemeal from a few vendors and fail audits.
solution: Hardware keys plus a cached-token offline mode and a shared-workstation login flow, with an agency-level compliance dashboard and audit-ready evidence. Onboard officers in minutes through mobile driver's license or badge-based identity proofing.
why_now: The deadline is fixed and less than 13 months out. Agencies are starting budget cycles now, and state CJIS systems agencies will begin enforcing.
revenue_model: $8-15 per user per month or a per-agency package of $6-30K per year, plus hardware sold at cost plus margin.
non_obvious_insight: The real customer is the MSP serving 50 small agencies. One channel partner delivers dozens of deployments, and offline behavior is the differentiator that enterprise identity vendors will not build.
first_30_days: Partner with 2 MSPs that serve sheriffs. Prototype offline token caching on a rugged laptop. Run 3 no-cost pilots in agencies with upcoming CJIS audits.

title: Verbal-Promise Ledger for Mine Community Relations
one_liner: A voice-first, offline-capable phone tool that turns every promise a mine makes at community assemblies (Spanish, Quechua, Aymara) into a tracked commitment register the community can verify by WhatsApp.
customer: Heads of social performance and community relations at mid-tier copper and lithium operators and developers in Peru, Chile, Argentina and Bolivia. The second buyer is the E&S team at the lender or DFI (IFC, EXIM, DFC, export credit agencies). Budget is roughly $2-6k per month per project, charged to a risk or permitting line, not to IT.
problem: Insiders know that projects get blockaded over small, forgotten verbal promises, not over the headline issue. Examples are a promised well repair, a local-hire quota, or a dust-suppression schedule. The promise is made at a 2pm assembly and recorded on a paper acta, in a notebook, or in a WhatsApp voice note. Community-relations staff rotate every 12-24 months, contractors make their own promises, and nobody indexes the actas. Two years later the community says 'you promised' and shuts the road. The Las Bambas corridor closures, Jujuy lithium protests and Tia Maria all fit this pattern of trust debt. The mine cannot prove what it did or did not commit to, and neither can the community.
solution: Field officers record assemblies on a phone and snap a photo of the signed acta. Speech-to-text, tuned for Andean Spanish and human-checked for Quechua and Aymara, extracts discrete commitments: who promised what, to whom, and by when. Each one is assigned an internal owner and a due date. Community leaders get a receipt as a WhatsApp voice note or pictogram and can confirm, dispute, or mark it done. Ops managers and the CFO see 'commitment debt' aging, like a technical-debt dashboard. One-click exports meet IFC Performance Standard 1 and Equator Principles grievance and commitment register requirements. Community-side verification is the moat. It makes this a trust tool, not a surveillance tool.
why_now: Speech models are good enough for accented, code-switched Spanish, and usable for Quechua with a human in the loop. WhatsApp is universal in rural Andean communities. Lenders are demanding auditable social-license evidence for critical-mineral financings, including EU CRMA strategic projects and US DOE/DFC/EXIM deals. Argentina's RIGI regime is pulling lithium and copper projects into provinces with little consultation history. Peru and Chile have changed governments (2026), which reopens community negotiations. Staff turnover after the 2024-25 cost-cutting rounds has made institutional memory worse.
revenue_model: SaaS at $2-6k per month per project, plus a per-community onboarding fee ($1-3k). A one-off 'commitment debt audit' of historical actas is priced at $5-15k. Later, a lender-grade verified engagement score and a lender or insurer data licence.
non_obvious_insight: Conflict risk is mostly commitment debt, meaning unanswered small promises lost through staff rotation, not big ideological opposition. Buyers think they need sentiment analysis. What they need is a receipt system. Giving the community the receipt is what makes the mine's data credible to lenders and inspectors.
first_30_days: Through ex-colleagues, recruit two junior or mid-tier developers currently in a consultation round. Sell a $5-10k 'commitment debt audit': scan their last 12 months of actas and meeting minutes, and use an LLM plus a local linguist to extract every commitment and flag the overdue ones. This works with no integration, just PDFs and photos. The overdue list is usually shocking, and it converts to a SaaS pilot for the next assembly round. Use a WhatsApp Business API bot and an offline recorder app for v1. Do not build a custom platform yet.

title: Robotic Pack-to-Cell Teardown for E-Bike Fleets
one_liner: A robot cell driven by a vision-language-action model that opens e-bike and scooter packs, tests every cell, and regrades them for low-cost storage.
customer: Delivery-app fleet operators, e-bike and scooter share operators, battery-swap networks and repair shops (pay per pack), with buyers of graded cells for stationary storage.
problem: Micromobility packs are the high-volume end-of-life lithium stream arriving now, while EV end-of-life will not dominate until after 2040. Manual teardown is dangerous and slow, so packs go to shredders at low value or sit in shops as fire risks.
solution: A cell with a robot foundation model fine-tuned on pack disassembly with force feedback. It cuts nickel strips, pulls cells, tests each one (IR and impedance), grades A/B/C, and repackages A-grade cells for stationary storage or tools. C-grade goes to recyclers. It starts as a manual-plus-robotic service in one city.
why_now: 2025-26 robot foundation models made unstructured manipulation tasks feasible, and e-bike fire scrutiny gives fleets a reason to pay.
revenue_model: Fee per pack processed, plus margin on graded cells, plus recycler payments for C-grade.
non_obvious_insight: Recyclers built for EV packs face feed that is 15 years late. E-bike packs are small enough that a robot cell amortizes quickly, and their cells are far from dead.
first_30_days: Contract with 2 fleet operators or a swap network in NYC or LA. Rent a bench with a fire-safe enclosure and cell testers. Process 500 packs manually to build the dataset and unit economics before adding the robot.

title: Sewage Nielsen: Wastewater Consumption Index
one_liner: Weekly per-capita consumption of alcohol, nicotine, cannabis and caffeine, measured from metabolites in city wastewater and sold to alt-data funds and regulators as a Nielsen for vices.
customer: Alt-data-buying hedge funds and long-only consumer analysts covering alcohol, tobacco and nicotine pouches, cannabis and energy drinks. Secondary: state cannabis and tax regulators who want to size legal versus illicit share, and cannabis operators or beverage companies buying custom market studies.
problem: Investors debating whether GLP-1 drugs and Gen Z are actually cutting alcohol, or whether nicotine pouches and cannabis are cannibalizing other products, rely on lagging, self-reported or scanner data. Those sources miss the illicit, gray-market, direct-to-consumer and cash segments. Regulators cannot measure the illicit cannabis share either.
solution: Composite-sample assays at 15-25 wastewater treatment plants across major metros, run weekly by a partner analytical lab (LC-MS/MS). Measure alcohol (ethyl sulfate), nicotine (cotinine), cannabis (THC-COOH) and caffeine metabolites. Normalize with population markers and flow to get per-capita consumption estimates. Only report at sewersheds serving 50k+ people, which handles privacy. Deliver as a weekly index via API and CSV with methodology notes. Sell a historical series built from archived samples.
why_now: The GLP-1 alcohol-reduction debate is a live equity question. Nicotine pouches and cannabis regulation are moving fast. Wastewater programs built with pandemic-era public health funding are shrinking or uncertain, which leaves utilities, university labs, sampling gear and freezer archives idle and open to co-funding. Alt-data budgets keep growing and funds want signals with no retail-panel bias.
revenue_model: Alt-data subscription of roughly 60-250k USD per year per fund, with tiered metro coverage. Government and regulator contracts (illicit-market sizing). Custom brand or category studies of 25-100k USD. Later, per-sewershed expansions paid by cities as a public-health co-benefit.
non_obvious_insight: Sewage is the only consumption panel that cannot be gamed, self-reported or missed by scanner data, because it captures what people actually consume regardless of channel. The science has been used by European drug-monitoring networks for 15 years, but nobody has packaged it as a consumer-sector economic indicator. Pandemic-era freezer archives of stored samples let you sell a multi-year backtestable history on day one, which is the thing quant buyers require before they will pay.
first_30_days: Partner with a university lab that already has validated LC-MS/MS methods for these metabolites and old COVID-monitoring relationships with treatment plants. Sign MOUs with 3-5 plants. Run assays on archived samples to build a 2021-2025 backtest series for those sewersheds. Pitch 15 alt-data funds and data-aggregator marketplaces with the backtest chart of one hook (for example alcohol per-capita against local retail sales). Launch a pilot at 5 sewersheds with 2-3 design-partner funds paying pilot fees. Note that the plan depends on plant access agreements and lab throughput.

title: FinOps for Open-Banking Data Spend
one_liner: Bank data access is turning into a metered cost. Do for aggregator bills what cloud FinOps did for AWS bills.
customer: Fintech lenders, budgeting apps and payroll and EWA apps spending $200k-$10M per year on aggregators (Plaid, MX, Finicity) and direct bank APIs.
problem: The CFPB 1033 rule is stayed, and a rewrite sent to OIRA on 2026-08-06 may let banks charge aggregators past a free-request threshold (PYMNTS). Developers over-poll accounts and pay per connection and per refresh, and a fee threshold would create sudden bill shock. Nobody owns the cost line.
solution: A proxy and observability layer that dedupes and caches pulls, replaces polling with webhooks and event-based refreshes, refreshes only when a decision needs fresh data (underwriting, payday), benchmarks vendor mix and price, and forecasts spend under proposed fee scenarios.
why_now: Regulatory uncertainty is at its peak, states like New York are proposing their own regimes, and fintechs face margin pressure. Any fee threshold in the rewrite turns data access into variable cost of goods sold.
revenue_model: 15-20% of verified savings (gainshare) or $2k-$10k per month SaaS.
non_obvious_insight: Data-access cost is becoming a real COGS line that finance teams can't yet see. My hypothesis is that dedupe and smarter refresh timing alone save 20-40%, so the first step is an audit that verifies it. A fee threshold makes that savings pool bigger.
first_30_days: Offer a free aggregator bill audit to 20 fintechs (they share invoices and usage exports). Quantify wasteful pulls, convert two to a 15% gainshare agreement, and publish the anonymized benchmark.

title: Stablecoin Depeg and Freeze Cover
one_liner: GENIUS made stablecoins legal, not insured. Sell corporate treasurers parametric cover for issuer depeg, redemption suspension and wallet freezes so their risk committees will approve holding balances.
customer: Treasurers and CFOs at mid-market and payments companies holding $1M-$100M in USDC or USDT, including corporate clients of the new Citi and Coinbase flow.
problem: GENIUS gives holders priority claims but no deposit insurance. USDT is about $140B and USDC about $74B, the Senate Democrats' Tether report alleges $2B of Iranian flows against $550M frozen, and Bitcoin has drawn down about 50%. Auditors and risk committees want risk transfer, and there is none.
solution: Parametric cover that pays when a named stablecoin trades below a threshold (for example $0.985) for 72 hours on defined venues, when redemption is suspended beyond a set number of days, or when the issuer freezes the insured's wallets. Price from on-chain and reserve-attestation data and place capital with crypto-native and traditional ILS providers through an MGA.
why_now: Corporate flows went live on 2026-09-28. The Fed proposed reserve and capital rules on 2026-09-24, making issuer risk legible. Annual volume is over $90T, and softening reinsurance gives capital a reason to look at new risks.
revenue_model: Premium of about 0.3-1.0% of covered balance per year, MGA commission, and a paid reserve-monitoring and rating subscription.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders assume regulated equals safe, but corporate risk committees need transferred risk, not comfort. The trigger is objective and cheap to verify, and an independent reserve monitor and rating is a valuable by-product.
first_30_days: Publish a public reserve and peg-monitoring dashboard as a lead magnet and pitch 20 treasurers. Negotiate a first $10M of quota-share capacity from a crypto-native capital provider and pilot with a payments company holding customer float.

title: Blinded Diligence Bureau for AI-Biotech Financiers
one_liner: A buyer-paid, blinded prospective testing service that tells pharma BD teams, royalty funds and lenders whether an AI drug-discovery platform's claims hold up in a neutral wet lab.
customer: Pharma BD&L and search-and-evaluation teams, corporate VCs, venture lenders, synthetic-royalty funds and crossover investors underwriting AI biotechs.
problem: AI-biotech capital is enormous ($6B+ in 2026, including Isomorphic's $2.1B and Chai's $400M). Deals are headlined in biobucks: Genentech-Earendil is $55M upfront against $1.5B+ total. Buyers still rely on vendor-supplied retrospective slides. The public competitions (Adaptyv, Anthropic x Adaptyv) test protein binding only and are public, not confidential diligence on a buyer's own targets. Small-molecule, antibody and ADMET claims have no neutral test.
solution: A custom blinded bake-off. The buyer picks 5-20 targets or properties (binding, potency, developability, ADMET). Two to four shortlisted vendors submit designs under NDA. Neutral partner labs assay them blind: an Adaptyv-style lab for binders, a CRO for ADMET. The buyer gets a ranked result, hit rate versus controls, a free open-model baseline (Boltz, BindCraft and similar) and a red-flag memo. Vendors never pay for ranking.
why_now: Frontier-lab designs hit about 27% in Adaptyv's blind test (1,320 designs, 16 targets, 354 binders), so 'does it beat free open models' is now the right question. Software-only AI shops are wobbling (Schrodinger cut staff), and mega-rounds attract generalist money that cannot judge the science. At least 12 funded biotechs sold for $1B+ this year, so acquirers need fast technical diligence. Adaptyv just raised $40M, so neutral wet-lab capacity can be rented.
revenue_model: $60-250k per blinded engagement, $150k/year retainers for funds that see 10+ platforms, and anonymized aggregate 'state of AI design' reports as a secondary product.
non_obvious_insight: 'Beats a free open-source baseline' is the question nobody prices. Buyer-paid independence, with no vendor fees, is the only credible model. Neutral labs already exist to rent, and consultancies lack lab access. Competitions such as Adaptyv's are partners and lead sources, not rivals, because they are public and binder-only.
first_30_days: Pitch 5 corporate-VC and BD teams currently evaluating platforms and sign 2 pilots at $40-60k. Rent capacity from an Adaptyv-style lab and one CRO. Design a 10-target panel with 3 anonymized vendors plus an open-model baseline. Publish the methodology to build trust.

title: Paper-Mill Shield for Diamond Open-Access Journals
one_liner: An Open Journal Systems plugin and service that screens incoming manuscripts and reviewers using public research detectors, and hands volunteer editors a plain-language decision memo.
customer: Library-publishing programs, university presses, national journal platforms and scholarly societies that run dozens to thousands of small journals on Open Journal Systems (OJS). The buyer is the consortium or library publishing unit, not the individual journal, whose budget is close to zero.
problem: Paper mills, LLM-generated manuscripts and fake reviewer identities hit small journals run by volunteer editors. Big publishers have enterprise integrity suites (Clear Skies, the STM Integrity Hub). Small journals have nothing, and a single wave of fraudulent papers can get them delisted from Scopus or Web of Science.
solution: Submission-time screening chained from public sources: Problematic Paper Screener fingerprints (tortured phrases, ChatGPT tells), reference-list checks against the Retraction Watch database now openly available through Crossref, citation-cartel and author-network anomalies via OpenAlex, and reviewer-suggestion checks (ORCID, email domain and institution mismatches). Flagged items go to a human integrity analyst. The editor receives a one-page memo with evidence and a suggested action, not a score. Includes a backlist audit product.
why_now: Paper-mill scale is now documented (the Problematic Paper Screener scans on the order of 130M publications weekly and has fed 1,000+ retractions). Retraction Watch data went open via Crossref. LLM text makes fakes cheap. Diamond open access is growing fast because of funder mandates, which means more volunteer-run journals with no integrity budget.
revenue_model: USD 3-10 per screened submission for individual journals. Consortium plans at USD 2-15k per year covering a platform's journals. Fixed-fee backlist audits per journal. Human analyst escalations billed hourly.
non_obvious_insight: The detectors already exist as free tools used by sleuths. What editors lack is accountability packaging: a defensible written memo they can cite when rejecting an author, and someone to escalate to. Sell decision memos to the consortium that hosts the journals, not detection scores to journals.
first_30_days: Build the pipeline as a command-line tool first, then an OJS plugin. Approach three library publishing programs and the PKP community forum. Offer 5 free backlist audits to journals that consent to anonymized findings. Publish a 'state of small-journal fraud' write-up from the audits as the PR hook. Sign one consortium pilot at a nominal fee.
